entries.meaning: From French Charles, from Old French Charles, Carles, from Latin Carolus, from and also reinfluenced by Frankish and Old High German Karl, from Proto-Germanic *karilaz (“free man”); compare the English word churl and the German Kerl. In reference to the Ecuadorian island, a clipping of the original name King Charles's Island, granted in honor of Charles II of England.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: Charles + -etta
entries.note: A female given name of African-American usage.

entries.meaning: From French Charline.
entries.note: A female given name from French, equivalent to English Charlene.

entries.meaning: 20th century variant of Charmian, or coinage from the noun charm with the -aine ending as in Elaine and Germaine.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage.

entries.meaning: Diminutive form of Ancient Greek χάρμα (khárma, “joy”). According to Plutarch, the name of a servant and advisor of Cleopatra.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From chartreuse.
entries.note: A female given name from English.

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Hindi चारु (cāru).

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Hindi चार्वी (cārvī), from Sanskrit चार्वी (cārvī), feminine of चारु (cāru).

entries.meaning: From Old English Ċealchȳþ, from cealc (“chalk”) + hȳþ (“landing place”).

entries.meaning: From Middle English Chestre, from Old English Ċeaster, from ċeaster (“a town or city, especially a Roman one”). The village in Nova Scotia is likely named after the city in Pennsylvania.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit चेतन (cetana).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit चेतना (cetanā).

entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Cheyenne, from Dakota šahíyena, from Dakota šaia (“to speak incoherently”), from Dakota ša (“red”) and Dakota ya (“to speak”).
entries.note: A female or male given name of modern American usage.

entries.meaning: Of Anglo-Norman origin, ultimately from Old French chesne (“oak”).
entries.note: A male given name of rare usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit छवि (chavi, “persona, image”).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit छाया (chāyā, “shadow, silhouette”).

entries.meaning: From Chinese 簡／简 (Jiǎn), 檢／检 (Jiǎn), or 劍／剑 (Jiàn). Alternatively, from 錢／钱 (Qián), 千 (Qiān), or 乾／干 (Gān). As a given name, from 建 (Jiàn), 健 (Jiàn), or 謙／谦 (Qiān). Doublet of Qian and Jian.
entries.note: A given name from Chinese.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Japanese ちはる
entries.note: A female given name from Japanese

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Japanese ちひろ (Chihiro).
entries.note: A unisex given name from Japanese.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Childebert, from Medieval Latin Childebertus, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Hildiberhtaz, from *hildiz (“battle, fight”) + *berhtaz (“bright, shining”).
entries.note: A male given name from Frankish, of historical usage, equivalent to English Hilbert, notably borne by various Frankish kings.

entries.meaning: From French Childéric, from Frankish *Hildirīk via Latin Childericus. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Hildirīks.
entries.note: A male given name of mainly historical use, borne by several kings of the Franks.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Chilpéric, from Medieval Latin Chilpericus, from Frankish *Helparīk (and partly through a Burgundian equivalent), from Proto-Germanic *Helparīks, from *helpaną (“help”) + *rīks (“king”).
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages, of historical usage, notably borne by various Frankish and Burgundian kings.

entries.meaning: African-American coinage.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage, of late 20th and early 21st century African-American usage, variant of Shaniqua.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit चिन्मय (cinmaya, “consciousness”).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Persian چراغ (čirāġ, čarāġ, “lamp, lightsource”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Persia often used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit चिरंजीव (ciraṃjīva, “immortal, long-lived”).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit चिरञ्जीवी (cirañjīvī, “immortal, long-lived”).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit चित्राङ्गदा (citrāṅgadā).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit चित्रसेन (citrasena).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Japanese ちよこ (Chiyoko).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Chlōtharius, from Frankish *Hlōdhari, ultimately from From Proto-Germanic *hlūdaz (“loud, famous”) + *harjaz (“commander, warrior”). Cognate with Old English Hloþhere, German Lothar.
entries.note: A male given name from Frankish, of historical usage, notably borne by various Frankish kings.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Chramnus, from Frankish *Hramn, Proto-West Germanic *hrabn, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hrabnaz (“raven”). Doublet of raven.
entries.note: A male given name from Frankish, of historical usage, notably borne by Chramn, a Merovingian prince.

entries.meaning: from Chris + -ie, through clipping of Christine or Christina
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given names Christina and Christine, sometimes also used as a formal given name

entries.meaning: Christopher or Chris + -o
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given names Christopher and Chris.

entries.meaning: Contraction of Christina and Christiana. Rare until the second half of the 20th century, reinforced by the German Christa.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Cristabell, Cristabelle, from Crist (“Christ”) + -bel (“beauty”) (see Belle).
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Christ + -bella, by analogy to Isabella and Arabella.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Rare non-standard spelling of Christine.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Cristien, from Old French chrestien, from Latin Chrīstiānus, from Ancient Greek Χρῑστιᾱνός (Khrīstiānós), from Χρῑστός (Khrīstós, “Christ, anointed [one]”) + Latin suffix -ānus. The older form is Christen. Doublet of cretin. By surface analysis, Christ + -ian.
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek found in England since the twelfth century.
entries.origin: Ancient Greek found in England since the twelfth century

entries.meaning: From Latin Chrīstiāna; a medieval literate form of the female name Christian. By surface analysis, Christian + -a.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Blend of Christian + Anne, coined as a feminine form of Christian.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Name of an early martyr, shortened from Latin Chrīstiāna (“Christian (woman)”). Doublet of Kirsten.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Christine. Doublet of Christina.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Late Latin Christophorus, from Koine Greek Χρῑστόφορος (Khrīstóphoros, “carrier of Christ”), from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós, “Christ”) + φόρος (phóros, “carrier, bearer”), from φέρειν (phérein, “to carry, to bear”) + -ος (-os, “-er: forming agent nouns”), from the legend of Saint Christopher carrying the infant Jesus across a river.
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Christopher + -a.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin [in turn from Ancient Greek], of rare usage.

entries.meaning: A feminine form of Latin Chrīstophorus. By surface analysis, Christophor + -a.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin [in turn from Ancient Greek], of rare usage.

entries.meaning: From chrysanthem(um) + -a.
entries.note: A female given name of rare usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Chrysippus, from Ancient Greek Χρῡ́σιππος (Khrū́sippos).
entries.note: A male given name of historical usage, notably borne by Chrysippus, an Ancient Greek Stoic philosopher of the Hellenistic period.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Chrȳsostomus, from Koine Greek Χρυσόστομος (Khrusóstomos, literally “golden-mouthed”), from χρυσός (khrusós, “gold”) + στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).
entries.note: A male given name from Latin [in turn from Ancient Greek], of rare usage.

entries.meaning: Variant spelling of Crystal.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Irish Ciarán.

entries.note: A male given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: From cinder + Italian -ella, as in little cinder girl. Compare French Cendrillon.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage.

entries.meaning: 20th-century variant spelling of Cindy.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Cynthia.

entries.meaning: Shortened from Lucinda and Cinderella. In the 20th century adopted as a pet form of Cynthia.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Cynthia and Lucinda; also used as a formal female given name.

entries.meaning: Unadapted borrowing from Somali Cismaan.
entries.note: A male given name in Somali, [Term?], equivalent to Osman.

entries.meaning: A less common spelling of Claire.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Claire, also a spelling variant of the English Clare.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Mac Fhlannchaidh (“descendant of a person named Red Warrior”), from flann (“blood-red”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Medieval English vernacular form of Clara, from the Latin clara, feminine of clarus (“bright, shining, clear”), a post-classical name made famous by the 13th century Saint Clara of Assisi. In Oxfordshire, from Clarora, a clay slope.
entries.note: A unisex given name from Latin, more often spelled Claire from the 20th century onward.

entries.meaning: Originally a ducal title of the English and British royal family, from Clārensis (“from the town of Clare”), (the town of Clare, Suffolk), although it has also been associated with Italian Chiarenza, Clarentza, &c., a former fortress and settlement in the medieval Frankish Principality of Achaea in Greece.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Elaborated form of Clare.
entries.note: A female given name of African-American usage, most popular in the mid-20th century.

entries.meaning: A fanciful variant of Clara, inspired by names like Annabel, Christabel or Isabel.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Clarisse, from Italian Clarissa, from Medieval Latin Clarissa (“Poor Clare”); see there for more. Doublet of Clarissa and Clarisse.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: From Clara + -inda.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Italian Clarissa, from Medieval Latin Clarissa; see there for more. Popularized in English by Samuel Richardson's 1748 novel Clarissa. Doublet of Clarisse.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin or Italian.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Clarisse, from Italian Clarissa, from Medieval Latin Clarissa (“Poor Clare”); see there for more. Doublet of Clarissa and Clarice.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: From Old English clerc (“clergyman; learned man”), whence also clerk.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Variant of Claude.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: In use from the 16th century. Borrowed from French Claude, from Latin Claudius, the name of a Roman gens. The clan name is traditionally said to be from Latin claudus (“lame”), but is most likely of Sabine origin.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: In use from the 16th century. Borrowed from Latin Claudia.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, masculine equivalent Claudius.

entries.meaning: French Claudine
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: From Latin Claudius. Doublet of Claude.

entries.meaning: From Dutch and German Claus, a contraction of Nicolaus (“Nicholas”). The spelling Klaus is from more modern German Klaus and other Germanic languages.
entries.note: A male given name from Dutch or from German [in turn from Ancient Greek].

entries.meaning: From a Middle English occupational name for a clay worker, or a habitational name, from Old English clǣġ (“clay”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Claytone, Cleyton, from Old English clǣġ (“clay”) + Old English tūn (“enclosure, settlement; town”). Analyzable as clay + -ton.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Cleanthēs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Κλεάνθης (Kleánthēs).

entries.meaning: From Latin Cloelia.

entries.meaning: From clemence, from Latin clēmentia (“mercy; mildness”).
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: From Late Latin Clēmēns (genitive Clēmentis), name of early saints and popes, from clēmēns (“merciful”). Doublet of Clement and San Clemente.
entries.note: A male given name, equivalent to English Clement.

entries.meaning: From Late Latin Clēmens (genitive Clēmentis), name of early saints and popes, from clēmens (“merciful”). Doublet of Clemens and San Clemente.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin, borne by an early pope and by several saints.

entries.meaning: Learned borrowing from Latin Clēmentīna. By surface analysis, Clement + -ina. Doublet of Clementine.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, variant of Clementine.

entries.meaning: From French Clémentine, from Latin Clēmentīna, from Clēmens (genitive Clēmentis), from clēmens (“merciful”). By surface analysis, Clement + -ine (feminine suffix). Doublet of Clementina.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin; feminine of Clement.

entries.meaning: Variant of Clemenson.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Diminutive + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Clementine.

entries.meaning: From Clementine + -y.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Clementine.

entries.meaning: Shortened from Cleopatra or a variant of Clio. The rare male name derives from names of Ancient Greek origin such as Cleon and Cleopas.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Κλέων (Kléōn), from κλέω (kléō, “to recount, celebrate”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Κλεοπᾶς (Kleopâs), contracted form of Κλεόπᾰτρος (Kleópătros).
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Cleopatra, from Latin Cleopatra, from Ancient Greek Κλεοπάτρα (Kleopátra), meaning "glory of her father", from κλέος (kléos, “glory”) + πατήρ (patḗr, “father”).
entries.note: A given name of women in the Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt; notably Queen Cleopatra VII of Egypt (69–30 BCE); last of the Ptolemy line.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Clētus, short form of the papal name Anaclētus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάκλητος (anáklētos, “invoked”, from ἀνακαλέω (anakaléō) + -τός (-tós)).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: The given name is from shortenings of the diminutives. The surname is from the noun cliff.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Clifford or Clifton.

entries.meaning: From Old English clif (“cliff”) + ford (“ford”), a dweller at the ford by the steep bank.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: *Literally meaning "town by a cliff." From Old English clif (“cliff”) + tūn (“town”). Analyzable as cliff + -ton. *In Oregon County, Missouri, from Cliff + -ton. From being named after a Cliff, or which may be clipped to Clif.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Diminutive of Clinton. The Yorkshire place name is from Old Danish klint.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: * (English habitational surname): A habitational surname, derived from places named Glinton ("town on a hill") or Glympton ("settlement on the River Glyme"), from Old English [Term?] + tun (“enclosure, homestead, town”), equivalent to the modern -ton. * (given name): Derived from the surnames. * (DeWitt County): Named after DeWitt Clinton.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, of 19th century and later usage.

entries.meaning: From the Ancient Greek Κλειώ (Kleiṓ). The award and car model were named after the goddess.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Irish Clíona.
entries.note: A female given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek κλειτός (kleitós), from κλέω (kléō, “to celebrate”) + -τος (-tos, verbal adjective suffix).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Italian Clorinda.
entries.note: A female given name from Italian, of rare usage.

entries.meaning: A Latinate form of the French Clotilde, of Germanic origin (Proto-Germanic *Hlūdahildiz).
entries.note: A female given name from the Germanic languages; of mostly historical use in the Anglo-Saxon world.

entries.meaning: From French, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish Clotilde, from Proto-Germanic *Hlūdahildiz.
entries.note: A female given name from French, Italian, Portuguese, or Spanish, of rare usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Clovis, from Frankish *Hlōdowig, the same Germanic source as French Louis, Dutch Lodewijk and German Ludwig, see there for further information. Doublet of Louis and Ludwig. The New Mexican city was named after a Frankish king; the Native American site and culture were named after this city.
entries.note: A male given name borne by several prominent people in Frankish/French and Germanic history.

entries.meaning: From Scottish Gaelic Cluaidh, the name of a river in Scotland, of uncertain origin. Possibly influenced by clut (“the cleansing one”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the place name (the River Clyde in Scotland).

entries.meaning: Feminine form of Latin Cloelius.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Knout, from Old English Cnut, from Old Norse Knútr.
entries.note: A male given name from Old Norse, a historical spelling of Canute (Scandinavian Knut) in historical context.

entries.meaning: Shortened form of Jacobus, Latin form of Jacob.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: From the Italian Coco, a surname derived from Sicilian cocu (“cook”).
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: A spelling variant of Cody.
entries.note: A unisex given name.

entries.meaning: A spelling variant of Cody.
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname

entries.meaning: * (Jewish): Variant of Cohen. * (given name): As a modern given name, also a variant of Koen.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Hebrew כֹּהֵן (kohén, “cohen”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From a Germanic personal name, composed of Proto-Germanic *kōlaz (“cool, cold; calm”) and *berhtaz (“bright”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From either the Old Norse personal name Koli or kol (“charcoal”) + býr (“settlement”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: The surname is variously from: # A nickname from Old English col (“coal, coal-black”), # A patronymic from Nicholas (see also Coles, Colson, Colle). # A variation of Cowell (which itself has several origins). # As an Irish and Scottish Gaelic surname, variant of McCool. # As a German surname, Americanized from Kohl. # As a Dutch surname, Americanized from Kool.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: (given name): * Coll + -in. Diminutive of Coll, a medieval short form of Nicholas. * It has also been used to anglicize Irish Coileán and Scottish Gaelic Cailean.
entries.note: A male given name

entries.meaning: Clipping of Nicholas
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Nicholas, of rare usage. A medieval English short form of the male given name Nicholas; very rare today.

entries.meaning: From the word colleen, from Irish cailín (“girl”), not used as a name in Ireland. Colleen can also be interpreted as a variant of Coleen, which was a product of marketing by the Hollywood film industry (to promote a new starlet in the 1920s).
entries.note: A female given name from English or Irish.

entries.meaning: Coll + -in. A spelling variant of Colin. From a medieval diminutive of Coll, a diminutive of Nicholas.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Nicholas, from Ancient Greek, variant of Colin.

entries.meaning: * As an English surname, variant of Colin. * As an Irish and Manx surname, from Ó Coileáin (“descendant of Coileán”), see Cullen, McQuillan, and McCallion. * As a French surname, Americanized from Collin and Colette. * As a Slovene surname, Americanized from Kolenc, from koleno (“knee”) and the obsolete kolenc (“nipplewort”).
entries.note: An English surname originating as a patronymic from the given name Colin.

entries.meaning: From Irish Colm, from Late Latin Columba (literally “dove”), the name of a sixth century saint, one of the patron saints of Ireland and Scotland. Doublet of Calum.
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: From the Irish saints' name Colmán, diminutive of Colm, from Latin columba (“dove”).
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: From colt, as a nickname or occupational name for someone who looked after horses and asses. The given name may also be short for Colton. The revolver is named after American inventor Samuel Colt (1814–1862).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Modern re-spelling of Colton.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Old English cola (“coal”) + tun (“settlement”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Latin columbus (“a dove”). Doublet of Colombo. The common noun and verb are references to the Italian explorer.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: From the English word comfort.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Borrowed from Latin Commodus, ultimately Latin commodus (“suitable; convenient”).
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: From Old English Cumbtūn. Equivalent to combe (“valley”) + -ton (“town”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Irish Conán, from Middle Irish Conán, from Primitive Irish ᚉᚑᚅᚐᚅᚅ (conann), a derivative of Proto-Celtic *kū (“dog”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ.
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: From Latin concordia (“concord”).
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Learned borrowing from New Latin Cōnfucius, from Mandarin 孔夫子 (Kǒng Fūzǐ, honorific title, literally “Master Kong”) + Latin -ius.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Anglicised from Irish Conlao, Conlaodh, from Old Irish Conláed. Saint Conláed was an Irish hermit and the first Bishop of Kildare.
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: Anglicization of Irish Ó Conghalaigh and Ó Conghaile, patronyms of Conghalach. Doublet of Connolly
entries.note: A male given name from Irish, transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Irish Conall.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Diminutives + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Constance or, rarely, of Concepción.

entries.meaning: The first name is from Irish Conchúr, Conchobhar, from Old Irish Conchobar (“lover of hounds”). The surname is from Irish Ó Conchúir (“descendant of Conchúr”).
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: From Irish Conchúr, from Old Irish Conchobar (“lover of hounds”).
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: A variant of German Konrad, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Kōnirād, from *kōnī (“bold, brave”) + *rād (“counsel”). Cognate of Old English Cēnrēd, Dutch Koenraad and Icelandic Konráð.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: Derived from Latin Cōnstantia. Doublet of Constantia.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Learned borrowing from Latin Cōnstantia. Doublet of Constance.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, of rare usage.

entries.meaning: From Latin Cōnstantīnus, the name of Roman emperors, Latin cōnstāns (“constant, steadfast”). Doublet of Konstadinos.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: From Latin Cōnstantīna and Greek Κωνσταντίνα (Konstantína).
entries.note: A female given name from Latin or Greek.

entries.meaning: From Latin Cōnstantīnus, the name of Roman emperors, notably that of Constantine the Great, Latin cōnstāns (“constant, steadfast”). Doublet of Konstadinos.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Probably a corruption of the personal name Constantine.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: From Spanish Consuela, a variant of Consuelo.
entries.note: A female given name from Spanish [in turn from Latin].

entries.meaning: Anglicization of Welsh Conwy
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Cooper.
entries.note: Diminutive of Cooper. A male given name.

entries.meaning: Perhaps from a short form of the personal name Jacob + -son.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Apparently brought up in English literature by James Fenimore Cooper in The Last of the Mohicans (1826), but compare a female heroine of this name in Jean-François Marmontel's Les Incas (1777) and the Ancient Greek epithet Κόρη (Kórē) for Περσεφόνη (Persephónē). It could also refer directly to κόρη (kórē, “maiden”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From coral.
entries.note: A female given name from English.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Coralie.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: An elaborate form of Coralie, itself derived from coral. Name of a character in Adolphe Adam's opera Le toréador.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage.

entries.meaning: An Anglo-Norman nickname from corb (“crow”), or shortened from the Corbinian, the name of a Frankish eighth-century saint, probably from Latin corvus (“crow, raven”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Shakespeare's spelling of a historical British name appearing as Cordeilla, etc., possibly derived from the Latin saint's name Cordula.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: From Late Latin Cordula, name of a companion of Saint Ursula, associated with Latin cor (“heart”) (genitive singular cordis).
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κόρη (kórē, “maiden”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek, probably from κόρη (kórē, “girl, maid, daughter”); compare kore.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From the French equivalent of Corinna, from Ancient Greek κόρη (kórē, “girl, maiden, daughter”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Irish, from Old Irish Cormac.
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: From the Old Irish given name Cormac. The town in Newfoundland is named after explorer and entrepreneur William Epps Cormack (1796 - 1868).
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: From Scottish Gaelic or from Irish Cormac, from Old Irish Cormac, Corbmac, from corb ("chariot") + mac ("son"). Many books also connect the name to an Irish word for "raven".
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: From Latin Cornēlia, name of a famous Roman matron, feminine form of the gens name Cornelius; in continental Europe, also a feminine form of the saint's name Cornelius.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin in quiet use since the 18th century.
entries.origin: Latin in quiet use since the 18th century

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Cornēlius.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: From Cornwall, spelling conflated with the Latin family name Cornelius.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: All ultimately from Latin corōna (“crown”). * (Corona, California): From Spanish corona (“crown, wreath”), chosen to play upon a unique feature of the city, the one-mile diameter drive that circled the center of the town. * (Corona, New Mexico): * (Corona, South Dakota): May be a transfer from Corona, Queens. * (Corona, Queens): One theory is that it was renamed by music producer Benjamin W.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Scottish Gaelic coire (“cauldron, boiler; corrie”), which denotes a bowl-shaped geographical feature similar to a cirque.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, of occasional usage.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek κόρη (kórē, literally “Maiden”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek κόρυδος (kórudos, “crested lark”).
entries.note: A male given name from Greek, notably used as a stock name for a shepherd in pastorals, in particular a shepherd whose love for a boy is described in Virgil's Eclogues.

entries.meaning: From Italian, a feminine form of Cosimo.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Latin Cosmas, from Ancient Greek Κοσμᾶς (Kosmâs), from κόσμος (kósmos). Doublet of Cosmo and related to cosmos.
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek of mostly historical use.
entries.origin: Ancient Greek of mostly historical use

entries.meaning: Borrowed by Scotland from Italy in the 18th century. An Italian variant of Cosimo, from the name Cosmas of a saint (martyred with his brother Damian in the fourth century), from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “order, ordered universe”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Latin Curtenus, from curtus (“short”), via Norman.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Variant of Courtenay, an aristocratic Norman surname derived from place names in Normandy, from Latin Curtenus, a personal name from curtus (“short”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Variant of Colling, a personal name which denoted an early owner of the properties.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Patronymic surname from Cocke + -son.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: From craig (“rock”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Κράντωρ (Krántōr), from κράντωρ (krántōr), agent noun of κραίνω (kraínō, “accomplish, fulfil”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek, of historical usage, notably borne by Crantor of Soli.

entries.meaning: From the Old English personal name Creoda.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Variant of Crichton.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Used by Geoffrey Chaucer, also by Shakespeare in Troilus and Cressida (1602), from Italian Criseida (which Boccaccio mistakenly substituted for Briseida (“Briseis”)), from Ancient Greek Χρυσηΐς (Khrusēḯs), from Ancient Greek χρυσός (khrusós, “gold”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Crewe in Cheshire, Old Welsh criu (“weir”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Christopher, Christian, Christine, and their variants.
entries.note: A unisex given name. A male given name. Diminutive of Christopher.

entries.meaning: From Latin Crispinus, derivative of the Roman family name Crispus (“curly”). Alternatively, contraction of Crispus (“hair”) and pinus (“pine”), according to Miraculum Quo Beata Maria Subvenit Guillelmo Crispino
entries.note: A male given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Latin Crispus, a Roman gens name from crispus (“curly”).
entries.note: A male given name from Latin of mostly historical use.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish Cristina.
entries.note: A female given name from Italian, Portuguese, or Spanish, equivalent to English Christina.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Spanish Cristóbal.
entries.note: A male given name from Spanish, an anglicized spelling of Spanish Cristóbal.

entries.meaning: From Latin Croesus, from Ancient Greek Κροῖσος (Kroîsos), from Lydian.
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek, of historical usage, notably borne by

entries.meaning: From Old English croft (“enclosure”) + tūn (“farmstead”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Old Norse kross (“cross”) + býr (“settlement”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Perhaps from French Crusiaux, a topographic surname from a diminutive of creux (“hollow”), or alternatively a variant of Croiseau, a habitational surname.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From crystal + -ia.
entries.note: A female given name of rare usage.

entries.meaning: From crystal + -ina, perhaps after crystalline (compare Crystalline).
entries.note: A female given name of rare usage.

entries.meaning: From crystalline.
entries.note: A female given name of rare usage.

entries.meaning: From Spanish Cuauhtémoc, from Classical Nahuatl Cuauhtemoc (“One That Has Descended Like an Eagle”).
entries.note: A male Mexican given name.

entries.meaning: Anglicized from the Irish Irish Coilean, from Irish coileán (“pup, youth, trickster”), Old Irish cuilén (“pup, cub”), from Proto-Celtic *kolignos (“whelp”), possibly of non-Indo-European origin.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: From Scottish Gaelic cuilinn.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Persian کامران (kâmrân).
entries.note: A transliteration of the Persian male given name کامران (kâmrân).

entries.meaning: From Old French corteis and curteis (Modern French courtois (“polite, courteous”). Doublet of courteous.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Irish cuisle (“pulse”); compare acushla, macushla.
entries.note: A female given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: Altered form of the personal name Cuthbert.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Name of early English saints, from Old English Cūþbeorht (“brightly known, famous”).
entries.note: A male given name from Old English.

entries.meaning: Occupational surname from cutler.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Shortening.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Cyril.

entries.meaning: A 20th-century variant of Sybil or Sibyl.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Often short for Cydney, a variant of Sydney/Sidney.
entries.note: A male given name

entries.meaning: Learned borrowing from Latin Cylōn or its etymon Ancient Greek Κῠ́λων (Kŭ́lōn).
entries.note: A male given name of historical usage. Cylon of Athens, an Athenian noble who attempted a coup in either 636 BCE or 632 BCE.

entries.meaning: 20th-century variant spelling of Cindy.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Cynthia.

entries.meaning: 20th-century variant spelling of Cindy.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Cynthia.

entries.meaning: 20th-century variant spelling of Cindy.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Cynthia.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Cynthia, from Ancient Greek Κυνθία (Kunthía), feminine of Κύνθιος (Kúnthios, “Cynthian (of or pertaining to Mount Cynthus, a mountain of Delos, celebrated as the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis)”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Latin Cyriacus, from Koine Greek Κυριακός (Kuriakós), from κυριακός (kuriakós, “related to the Lord, belonging to the Lord”), from Ancient Greek κύριος (kúrios) + -ακός (-akós, “-ac: forming adjectives”).
entries.note: A male given name from Koine Greek.

entries.meaning: Via Late Latin Cȳrillus, from Ancient Greek Κύριλλος (Kúrillos), from κύριος (kúrios, “lord, master”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek; best known for a ninth century missionary to the Slavs.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Cȳrus, from Ancient Greek Κῦρος (Kûros), from Old Persian 𐎤𐎢𐎽𐎢𐏁 (kuruš). As a saints' name it has been identified by folk etymology with Ancient Greek κύριος (kúrios, “lord”).
entries.note: A male given name from Old Persian.
